paragraphs: Here's what this psalm teaches, friend. When people treat you unfairly, you don't have to carry it alone, and you don't have to hide it. David says it plain: they laid their net "without cause" (Psalm 35:7). Then he takes the whole mess straight to the LORD, asking Him to "Contend with my opponents" (Psalm 35:1). Honest prayer isn't a sign of weak faith, it's what faith sounds like when it hurts.

Notice what David does with the pain. He says he mourned for these people like a friend or brother, and then they gathered in glee when he stumbled (Psalm 35:13-15). He asks, "How long, O Lord, will You look on?" (Psalm 35:17). I think that's one of the most honest questions a hurting person can ask, and God lets it stay in the Bible. And look at what David hangs on to in the middle of it: "O LORD, You have seen it" (Psalm 35:22). The crowd says their eyes have seen, but David knows whose eyes matter most.

Then the psalm keeps turning toward praise, and that's the part I want you to carry with you. Three times David promises thanks: his soul will rejoice, he'll give thanks in the great assembly, and his tongue will proclaim the LORD's righteousness "all day long" (Psalm 35:9, 18, 28). He doesn't wait for the problem to be gone to decide who he's going to trust. So when your own fight shows up, baker, bring it to the LORD out loud, and let your praise get started before the battle is done.
